opening.headline: When there are many opinions on introducing AI, but there is no agreement on where to start, the first case is selected based on three criteria: effectiveness, risk, and ease of implementation.
body: The sales team recommends using AI for proposals, the human resources team for evaluation, the customer support team for response, and the finance team for reports. It all seems reasonable, but without standards, it's easy for the most vocal department's work to be selected first. If you choose the wrong one, you may end up doing a task with little effect but high risk.

In this class, you will learn how to compare candidate work along two axes: effectiveness and risk. After looking at where the effects come from and where the risks come from, we directly place ten candidates. Finally, we compare the sales proposal draft with personnel evaluation comments to confirm our judgment in setting priorities and pilot scope.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the criteria for use case selection: effectiveness, risk, and ease of implementation
Candidate tasks can be divided into effectiveness and risk axes.
Can determine whether priorities are appropriate

screens.title: There are many opinions to introduce it, but where should we start?
screens.lead: Read the scene where requests from each department are piled up, and think about what would happen if you made decisions without standards.

visual.alt: A scene where each of the four departments presented in speech bubbles the work they wanted to do with AI.
labels: If there is no standard, the one with the loudest voice comes first.

paragraphs: The sales team suggests leaving the proposal drafting to AI. The human resources team requests evaluation comments, the customer support team requests responses, and the finance team requests reports. There have already been enough opinions to introduce it.

The problem is that there is no agreement on what to do first. If there are no criteria, the most vocal department jobs will be chosen first. If the task is small in effect but high in risk, the first case may fail and trust in the entire subsequent implementation may fall.
This lesson covers how to organize candidates by three criteria: effectiveness, risk, and ease of execution. The goal is to select the first case based on evidence.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Which of the four departments' requests should come first? For now, I will answer based on intuition, and after class is over, I will answer again based on the standard.

screens.outro: Let me start by thinking about my team’s candidate work.

screens.title: Three tasks the team wants to solve with AI
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.answer: The more time-consuming and repetitive a task is, the more effective it will be when reduced to AI. The first clue to effectiveness is repeatability and time taken. Doing it once has little effect.

items.prompt: Is it a big deal if you're wrong?
items.answer: The greater the damage, the higher the risk. Examples include documents that go out, decisions that affect individuals, and actions that are difficult to reverse. Risk is not viewed as the possibility of being wrong, but as the amount of damage that would result if you are wrong.

items.prompt: Are the materials and procedures already organized?
items.answer: You can start work right away when the data is gathered and the procedures are clear. This is ease of execution. Even if the effect is great, if the materials are scattered, it takes more time to prepare.

screens.outro: Three questions are three criteria. First, let's look at where the effect comes from.

screens.title: The Range of What AI Can Do: Sources of Effect
screens.lead: By selecting and expanding each item, you can see the scope of work that AI can help with and what kind of work effects it leads to.

items.title: Primary uses: questions, drafts, summaries, translations
items.body: ChatGPT Feature Overview Documents are primarily used to answer questions and explain concepts, write, rewrite, and summarize, suggest ideas, solve problems using logical reasoning, and translate between languages. This includes tasks such as summarizing meeting minutes, drafting documents, and translation.

items.title: Handling files and data
items.body: Upload documents, spreadsheets, and presentations to summarize or extract information. Data analysis features run your code in a secure environment to analyze and visualize tables, summarize trends, clean data, and make estimates. This is where the effectiveness of organizing internal data comes from.

items.title: deep research
items.body: Deep research combines multiple sources to create a structured report with citations. The document guides you to use it when you want to control your sources in multi-step, in-depth questioning. It is suitable for drafting strategic materials, literature research, or market research reports. A regular conversation may be faster for short queries.

items.title: Common features of highly effective work
items.body: It is most effective in tasks that are repetitive, time-consuming, and benefit from draft-level output. This is because it reduces the time a person spends from scratch, and allows people to focus on confirmation and correction.

items.title: Time is not the only effect
items.body: The benefits include not only time savings, but also quality and consistency. Another effect is that everything is organized in the same format and the variation in results that vary from person to person is reduced. Therefore, when evaluating effectiveness, we look at both the time taken and the uniformity of the results.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the source of the effect, let's look at where the danger comes from.

screens.title: Axis of Risk: Data and the Damage of Getting It Wrong
screens.lead: Select each tab to see the four axes that divide business risk.

visual.alt: A diagram showing the four axes that divide risk with four bars.
labels: Risk goes down with human review

tabs.label: the gravity of the decision
tabs.body: High-risk automated decisions without human supervision are also treated with caution in the OpenAI usage policy. Representative areas include employment, healthcare, finance, and law. The task of AI determining the treatment or rights of individuals is highly effective but carries high risks.

tabs.label: Personal information
tabs.body: When handling customer or employee information, input and retention conditions must be considered. Each provider has different conditions. For example, the Gemini API states that it retains prompts, input context, and output for 55 days to prevent abuse. For tasks involving personal information, we first check whether it can be de-identified before inputting it.

tabs.label: external disclosure
tabs.body: Incorrect information in documents that are sent out to the outside world can quickly become a reputation issue for the organization. There is an opportunity to correct errors in materials that are only used for internal reference, but it is difficult to correct documents once they are published.

tabs.label: execute permission
tabs.body: If an agent directly sends or changes an email, it is difficult to reverse. Agents executing tasks require approval and limited permissions before external transfers or changes. The mere presence of a confirmation window does not eliminate all risk. The broader the execution privileges, the greater the risk.

tabs.label: low risk work
tabs.body: Low-risk work is draft-intensive, with humans reading and modifying the results. The risk of the same task goes down if there is human review, and goes up if it is carried out immediately without review. Risk is not defined by the name of the task, but by where people engage.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified both axes, let's actually lay out the candidate tasks.

screens.title: Arrange the ten candidates on two axes: effectiveness and risk.
screens.lead: The table below divides the ten candidate tasks and one for comparison into benefits and risks. Read the reasons for your decision in each horizontal line.

data.notes: Do not start tasks that have little effect and are high risk. Do the high-impact, low-risk work first, and start the high-impact, high-risk work after you have a human review design in place.

screens.outro: Now that you know how to deploy, let's move on to an example that directly compares the two tasks.

screens.title: Commentary: Comparison of draft sales proposals and personnel evaluation comments
screens.lead: The instructor compares the two candidates on the same basis. Select the right arrow to see the steps one by one.

steps.title: compared to
steps.body: The two tasks to be compared are a draft sales proposal and a personnel evaluation comment. They both seem similar because they involve writing, but if you apply the same standards, the results will be different. Effectiveness, risk, and ease of implementation are compared in turn.

steps.title: Effect of Draft Proposal
steps.body: Drafting a sales proposal is very effective because it takes a long time to write, has a repetitive structure, and can use past proposals as data. This is a typical task where draft-level deliverables are helpful, and the material is already there, so it's easy to execute.

steps.title: Pitfalls of Draft Proposals
steps.body: Drafts are read and edited by humans, so they are written documents, not decisions. De-identifying customer information further reduces risk. However, the amount and promises must be verified by a person.

steps.title: Dangers of Evaluative Comments
steps.body: Personnel evaluations are decisions that directly affect individuals in the area of employment. When AI determines assessments without human supervision, it becomes closer to the high-risk automated decisions that policy calls into question.

steps.title: Effect of evaluation comments
steps.body: There is a time-saving effect in refining the text of evaluator comments. However, since the core judgment of evaluation is the responsibility of humans, it is difficult to accept the effect if most of the effect comes from leaving the judgment itself to AI.

steps.title: conclusion of comparison
steps.body: A draft proposal is a high-impact, low-risk solution that gives you a head start. Evaluative comments, although effective, are high risk and wait until a human review design is in place. Even for the same writing task, the magnitude of risk is different. You should judge the results not by the name of the task, but by who it impacts and how it affects them.

screens.outro: Let's now link this comparison to priorities and pilot scope.

screens.title: Commentary: Setting priorities and pilot scope
screens.lead: The instructor walks you through the process of converting comparison results into priorities and pilot scopes. Select the right arrow to see the steps.

steps.title: priority
steps.body: Put the draft sales proposal first. Personnel evaluation comments are subordinated until a human review design is in place. Deferred does not mean that you will not do it, but it means that you will start after preparations are completed, and the preparation conditions are also written down.

steps.title: Location of human review
steps.body: The proposal is sent after the person in charge reads the draft and confirms the figures and promises. A way to lower risk is to first determine the point at which human review will occur. It should not be a formal approval, but rather a confirmation of understanding and judgment of the content.

steps.title: pilot scope
steps.body: Start by narrowing it down to one team, one type of document, and a few weeks. If the scope is narrow, even if a problem occurs, the impact is small and the cause is easy to find. Look at the results and expand on them.

steps.title: What to See in the Pilot
steps.body: See how long it took, how much correction was made, what type of error it was, and whether data processing conditions were violated. We also record the amount of corrections and the types of errors, because looking only at the time can miss any loss of quality. If you use a tool with execution privileges, such as an agent, check the privilege range as well.

steps.title: Expansion after pilot
steps.body: If the pilot shows that time is reduced, the amount of revisions is within acceptable range, and there are no data condition violations, expand the same document type to other teams. If a problem appears, address the cause first before expanding the scope. Whether or not to expand is decided based on recorded evidence, not based on intuition, and the evidence is shared within the team.

steps.title: feasibility judgment
steps.body: It is valid if the priorities are explained in terms of effectiveness and risk, and others can reach the same conclusion using the same criteria. If you have to explain it by voice volume or personal preference, there is insufficient evidence.

screens.outro: Now that we've walked you through the entire prioritization process, let's summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Start with high-impact, low-risk tasks.
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class. Please answer the original question again based on which of the four departments' requests came first.

paragraphs: The first example starts with high-impact, low-risk tasks. Effects are seen in terms of time, quality, and consistency, while risks are seen in the severity of the decision, privacy, external disclosure, and execution authority. Add to this the ease of execution of seeing whether materials and procedures are organized, and organize candidates.

Tasks that are high-impact but high-risk are started after first designing a location for human review. In the first four department requests, the draft sales proposal comes first, and personnel evaluations take a back seat until a review design is in place. Start with a narrow pilot, such as one team, one document, or a few weeks, and expand based on the results.

callout.label: standards to remember
callout.text: Risk is determined not by the name of the job, but by where the human review is.

checks.intro: Summarize what you just learned by pairing your judgment with the candidate's work. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Match the following candidate tasks with judgments based on effectiveness and risk placement.
right: Human review and design come first
checks.explain: Start with high-impact, low-risk tasks. If the effect is large but the risk is high, review design comes first, and if the effect is small, it is left behind even if it is easy.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: What is the most appropriate basis for deciding to place personnel evaluation comments at a lower priority than the sales proposal draft?
options: The proposal does not contain any customer information
Appraisals are employment decisions that directly affect individuals and therefore carry high risk without human oversight.
There is nothing in evaluation comments where AI will save time
The draft proposal can be sent as is without anyone reading it.
checks.explain: Proposal drafting is a document that is read and edited by humans, but evaluation is an employment-related decision and is placed on the back burner until a design for human review is in place.

wrong.0: Customer information can also be included in proposals, further reducing risk through de-identification.
wrong.2: Comment sentences can save time, but the key issue is that the decision is left to the human.
wrong.3: The proposal is also sent after the person in charge confirms the figures and promises.

glossary.def: This is a repetitive, time-consuming task that benefits from draft-level output.
Even if there is a mistake, the damage is small and a person checks the results and makes corrections.
This is the point where humans check AI results before they are sent out or used to make decisions.
It is a narrowly defined pilot introduction scope, such as one team, one task, and a short period of time.
The materials and procedures are organized so you can get started right away.

misconceptions.myth: Just start with the most effective tasks.
misconceptions.fact: If the effectiveness is high but the risk is high, human review design comes first. Look at both effectiveness and risk, and start tasks with greater effectiveness and lower risk first.

misconceptions.myth: You can do any low-risk work.
misconceptions.fact: Low risk is an assessment based on human confirmation of the results. If you write directly without confirmation, the risk of the same task increases.

misconceptions.myth: It is effective only if you start as a warrior from the beginning.
misconceptions.fact: It is safer to gather evidence from a narrow pilot and expand it. If the scope is narrow, even if a problem occurs, the impact is small and the cause is easy to find.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Effectiveness is seen in terms of time, quality, and consistency, and risk is seen in the severity of the decision, privacy, external disclosure, and execution authority.
Determine the location of human review first.
Start with a narrow pilot and build and expand your base.
